newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada posts current account surplus, growth slow.
newsitem.headline: Canada posts current account surplus, growth slow.

text.p: Canada's balance of payments current account swung into surplus for the first time in more than a decade, the government reported Friday, but growth in the overall economy has disappointed economists.

The second-quarter current account surplus, reported by the government agency Statistics Canada, was mainly due to booming exports as the strengthening U.S. economy sucked in Canadian goods while Canadian imports fell.

The current account hit a surplus of $1.15 billion Canadian ($840 million U.S.) on a seasonally adjusted basis, after the first quarter's $1.62 billion deficit ($1.18 billion U.S.), according to Statistics Canada.

It was the first surplus since fourth quarter 1984 and may mark a turnaround in Canada's reliance on foreign borrowing, analysts said. Over the longer term, that turnaround will make it easier for the Bank of Canada to keep interest rates low and support the currency.

"The surplus is confirmed and larger than the market was looking for. This is clearly a long-run positive for the value of the Canadian dollar," said Andrew Spence, chief economist at Citibank Canada.
Despite that brighter outlook -- and seven successive cuts in interest rates by the central bank this year -- Canada's economic growth remains sluggish.
Real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by only 0.3 percent from the first quarter -- less than half what economists had expected -- as the economy sputtered in June.
"Economic growth halted in June after advancing the previous two months," the federal statistics agency said.
Economists are already talking of possible further interest rate reductions by the Bank of Canada because of low inflation and weak growth.

Royal Bank of Canada Deputy Chief Economist John Johnston said the current account numbers were positive but the weak GDP meant interest rates could fall further if next week's U.S. employment statistics are below expectations.
"We think there is a risk that the Bank of Canada may take the opportunity to cut rates another notch if the U.S. employment numbers are softer than expected," he said.
Sherry Cooper, chief economist at brokerage Nesbitt Burns, referred to the GDP numbers as "stunningly soft" and said it kept "further Bank of Canada (interest rate) easing hopes very much alive."
She noted that year-on-year GDP grew only 1.2 percent, barely matching population growth and running at a fraction of U.S. growth.

Unemployment in Canada is running at a politically embarassing 9.8 percent, prompting criticism by labour leaders of the deficit-cutting policies of Canada's Liberal government, led by Prime Minister Jean Chretien.
Chretien and his finance minister, Paul Martin, have relied on easier monetary policy, particularly lower interest rates, to stimulate growth.

They are banking on the private sector picking up the slack from government cuts. Slight signs of a growth revival have appeared in past months, but the latest GDP figures showed government services experienced a real decline of 1.2 percent in June, while the non-business sector fell 0.6 percent and the business sector edged up by just 0.1 percent.
